title: Private Deployments: VPC & On-Prem Reference Architectures, Packaging, Day-2 Ops, Upgrade & Rollback, Customer Requirements Library
author: Asha Patel
content:
Overview
========
This document consolidates the canonical guidance for Redwood Inference private deployments (VPC-hosted control plane and on-prem / air-gapped installs). It bundles: reference architectures, on-prem packaging guidance, a customer requirements library, day-2 operational runbooks, and formal upgrade & rollback procedures. Intended audience: SREs, Platform Engineers, Solutions Engineers, and Customer Engineering teams supporting private deployments.

Scope and intent
----------------
- Scope: VPC-managed private control plane, customer VPC peering, and fully on-prem (air-gapped) packaging.
- Intent: Provide a single reference that can be used during scoping, implementation, and ongoing operations; include concrete commands, configuration examples, and escalation paths.

Ownership
---------
- Primary owner: eng-private-deployments
- Reviewers: platform, security, and infra leads (listed above)
- Support path: customer-success -> solutions-eng -> eng-private-deployments -> eng-sre

Reference architectures (high-level)
------------------------------------
1) VPC-delegated deployment (recommended for cloud-first customers)
   - Components: private-control-plane (Redwood control plane components), customer-workload VPC, NAT gateways for egress, private endpoints for telemetry, cross-account IAM roles for resource provisioning.
   - Network flow: customer app -> private VPC (LB) -> Redwood inference nodes (in customer's account or dedicated account) -> model storage (S3-compatible) and metrics (Prometheus remote write).
   - Ownership: network/security owned by customer, runtime + orchestration owned by Redwood (for managed Dedicated offering) or by customer for self-hosted private deployments.

2) On-prem air-gapped reference (recommended for regulated / high-security customers)
   - Components: installer bundle, offline container registry, local object store (minio/ceph), local KMS/HSM integration, bastion for admin access, monitoring stack with remote-forwarding adapter.
   - Hard requirements: no outbound access from inference nodes unless explicitly allowed for updates; update channel via signed bundles.

Reference architecture diagrams (textual)
- VPC: customer-vpc [subnets: public, private] -> TGW/Transit -> Redwood-managed-account (private subnets) -> GPU node pool -> EFS/Model store
- On-prem: airgapped-segment -> bastion -> private-registry -> orchestrator (k8s) -> GPU pool -> local-object-store

Minimum customer requirements (checklist)
--------------------------------------
Use this checklist during scoping calls. Each item should be answered and recorded in the customer requirements ticket.
- Network
  - CIDR ranges available for deployment subnets (public/private)
  - NAT/egress requirements: outbound ports allowed (TCP 443 for control plane? yes/no)
  - VPN / Direct Connect / ExpressRoute availability
- Identity & Access
  - Cloud provider account IDs and IAM role names for cross-account provisioning
  - Service principal / client ID for installer automation
- Storage
  - S3 bucket (or compatible) with encryption at rest and lifecycle policies
  - Minimum capacity estimate (GB) and expected model pull frequency
- Secrets & Key Management
  - KMS access or HSM connectivity details
- Hardware
  - Supported GPU types (e.g., A10G, A100) and node-level RAM/disk minimums
  - Node counts for min/target/max pools for each inference profile
- Governance
  - Compliance constraints (SOC2, HIPAA, PCI) and required audit logs retention
- Contacts
  - Technical point of contact and escalation path

Packaging & installer guidance
----------------------------
- On-prem bundle: delivered as a signed tarball containing:
  1) Kubernetes manifests and Helm charts (or kustomize overlays)
  2) OCI images (exported as tarball) and a manifest with digests
  3) Signed release metadata (vulnerability scan summary, SBOM)
  4) Installer binary (platform installer) and documented CLI flags
- Install modes:
  - quickstart: single-node dev (not for production)
  - HA-k8s: production (3 master control-plane nodes, managed GPU node pools)
  - air-gapped: OCI images loaded from local registry; installer validates signatures locally
- Example installer invocation (HA-k8s):
  ./redwood-install --mode=ha --kubeconfig=/root/.kube/config \\   --registry-url=registry.local:5000 --bundle /tmp/redwood-bundle-v2028.2.tgz \\   --secrets-kms=projects/myproj/locations/global/keyRings/rw/cryptoKeys/rw-key
- Packaging requirements table:
  | Artifact | Required | Notes |
  |---|---:|---|
  | Signed bundle (tgz) | yes | Must include SBOM and GPG signature |
  | OCI image tarball | yes (air-gapped) | Use docker save format with digest manifest |
  | Helm charts | yes | Versioned with chartmuseum metadata |
  | Migration scripts | yes | idempotent, reversible where possible |

Day-2 operations (runbooks and best practices)
----------------------------------------------
- Monitoring & alerting
  - Metrics to collect: inference_latency_p50/p95, tokens_per_second, kv-cache-hit-rate, gpu_utilization, pod_restart_count
  - Recommended SLOs: p95 latency < 250ms for small models (<=2k context), GPU utilization target 60-75% for cost efficiency, error rate < 0.5%
  - Alerts (examples):
    - High latency (p95 > 300ms for 5m) -> P1 to oncall
    - Pod crashloop > 3 restarts in 15m -> P1 to platform team
    - Model download failures (> 10/min) -> investigate network/registry
- Backups and recovery
  - Config backup frequency: daily for cluster-level manifests, hourly for dynamic routing configs
  - Model artifacts: keep immutable copies in object store and enable object-lock where required
- Capacity scaling
  - Autoscaling policies: target CPU/GPU metrics with buffer of 20% headroom. For predictable workloads use scheduled scaling.
- Common day-2 procedures (numbered)
  1) Adding a new GPU node pool: run `redwood-cli nodepool create --profile=large --count=4 --gpu=A10G` and validate with smoke tests (see appendix).
  2) Replacing a failing node: cordon -> drain -> terminate -> ensure autoscaler provisions replacement.
  3) Rotating service credentials: follow the secret-rotation playbook and update Helm values with new secret references.

Upgrade & rollback procedures
---------------------------
Goals: minimize downtime, maintain SLOs, provide deterministic rollback path. All upgrades must be executed from a tracked release artifact.

Pre-upgrade checklist
- Verify current cluster state: `kubectl get pods --all-namespaces` (no > 5% pods in NotReady)
- Ensure backups completed and validated (etcd snapshot or object-store copies)
- Smoke tests passing against canary cluster
- Changelog and migration notes reviewed (DB/schema changes highlighted)

Canary upgrade pattern (recommended)
1) Prepare canary environment (10% capacity) in a different node pool or namespace.
2) Deploy release to canary and run full smoke + perf tests (latency and throughput).
3) Monitor for 30-60 minutes for regressions. Key metrics: p95 latency, error rate, kv-cache-hit-rate.
4) If canary stable, incrementally rollout to 25%, 50%, 100% using ProgressiveRollout controller.
5) Hold each step for at least the configured stabilization window (default 15 minutes).

Rollback procedure (on failed rollout)
1) Pause rollout controller.
2) Scale new pods to zero for the failing revision.
3) Re-apply previous stable release artifact: `helm rollback redwood-runtime 2` or `kubectl apply -f release-v1.3.2.yaml`
4) Validate with smoke tests and monitor SLOs.
5) Open incident report and schedule postmortem if P1.

DB/migration notes
- All database migrations must be backwards-compatible where possible. For breaking migrations, use two-step deploy: schema-first (compat layer) followed by application changes.

Testing & validation (smoke + perf)
---------------------------------
- Smoke test checklist (automated):
  - Basic API healthcheck returns 200 on /healthz
  - Simple generation request returns expected status and token consumption
  - Embeddings endpoint returns vector of expected length
- Performance validation: run the benchmark client with the production traffic profile (use `bench-runner` config in appendix). Validate p95 latency and throughput against defined SLOs.

Escalation & incident playbook (summary)
---------------------------------------
- P0 / P1: SLA-impacting incidents -> page oncall SRE, notify customer-success and account exec, open incident channel (#inc-<customer>)
- P2: degraded performance -> solutions-eng + eng-private-deployments owning remediation steps
- Communication: use status page template and provide ETA for mitigation.

Appendix A - Example config snippets
-----------------------------------
1) Minimal Helm values (production):
replicaCount: 4
image:
  repository: registry.local:5000/redwood/runtime
  tag: v2028.2
resources:
  limits:
    nvidia.com/gpu: 1
  requests:
    cpu: "2000m"
    memory: "16Gi"
nodeSelector:
  accelerator: a10g

2) Sample smoke test curl (health):
curl -sS -H "Authorization: Bearer ${RW_TOKEN}" https://private-redwood.example.com/healthz

3) Perf benchmark example (bench-runner config):
{ "concurrency": 16, "seq_len": 1024, "request_rate": 120 }

Appendix B - Rollout windows and maintenance windows
----------------------------------------------------
- Recommended maintenance window: 0200-0600 local time for updates requiring node reboots.
- For global customers, coordinate with customer-success to pick a low-traffic window and notify 72h in advance.

Appendix C - Contacts & ownership
--------------------------------
- Runbook owner: eng-private-deployments (oncall@redwood.example.com)
- Escalation: eng-sre (pager), security (security@redwood.example.com)
- Customer engagement: customer-success and solutions-eng assigned per account
